dry.text: Beneath the surface, solid coal still supports the roof. This cutaway follows one gob well as the longwall approaches. Watch rock, fractures, gas, and water as the face moves past.
The shearer cuts the coal while hydraulic shields protect the face. Behind them, the unsupported roof breaks and falls. Higher beds bend and separate over the gob.
The face has passed the well. A strong gas connection depends on roof movement and connected fractures — not face position alone.
Pale trails show gas moving toward the well. Methane itself is invisible. Fractures feed the casing under a pressure difference. ILLUSTRATIVE · not calibrated.
In the dry case there is no connected water. Gas keeps flowing through the fractured rock as the gob settles. No liquid head forms at the well.
Broken rock settles and the upper roof sags. Some fractures may stay open. ILLUSTRATIVE · not calibrated — real wells need measured production, water, and pressure.

Water enters faster than gas can remove it. Watch the pool rise at the well. Once the inlet is covered, liquid head adds backpressure — ILLUSTRATIVE √-law under fourteen kilopascals, not calibrated.
Liquid head consumes the assumed fourteen kilopascal drive, and gas delivery stops in this example. ILLUSTRATIVE · not calibrated — real loading needs measured pressures and water supply.
